newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish economy seen on track after Jan output data.
newsitem.headline: Polish economy seen on track after Jan output data.

text.p: The Polish economy began 1997 well with industrial output showing only a small seasonal fall and producer prices remaining a safe margin below consumer price inflation, analysts said on Tuesday.

The Central Statistical Office (GUS) said industrial output fell by 3.4 percent in January after a 2.1 percent rise in December with the year-on-year index dipping to 8.6 percent growth from 10.1 percent at the end of 1996.
GUS also said producer prices rose 1.9 percent last month, against a 0.5 percent increase in December, which pushed the year-on-year index up to 11.2 percent from 10.5 percent.

"It is a good start to the year with nearly 11 percent (year-on-year) growth in manufacturing and lower energy usage," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst at the government's Centre for Strategic Studies (CSS).
"This means manufacturing is becoming more energy and fuel efficient, which may signal that the economy will not stray far from 1996's six percent growth," Chroscicki said.
Year-on-year growth in manufacturing output dipped to 10.7 percent in January from 13.3 percent in December, while utility output growth amounted to year-on-year 2.8 percent last month.

"A three-month moving average of industrial output should remain around 10 percent this year with the January decline mainly caused by cold climatic conditions," said Andrzej Labenda, economist at Pekao SA brokerage in Warsaw.

Analysts said producer prices were still nearly seven percentage points lower than consumer prices, last at year-on-year 18.1 percent, and therefore would not become a driving force in consumer price growth for some time to come.
However, they said the gap between CPI and PPI would narrow as the devaluation of the Polish zloty nudges up import prices and keeps producer prices roughly stable in future months.

"The gap between producer and consumer prices will get smaller basically as a result of the exchange rate, which devalues the zloty and therefore increases price growth of imports," Pekao's Labenda said.
Some analysts said the zloty devalation constant, now at one percent per month against a basket of currencies, should be cut in the near future to keep producer prices downward bound.

But a strong exporters' lobby and the central bank, worried about a rapidly growing trade deficit, had suggested that this year's planned nine percent zloty devaluation target would be surpassed. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
